Section 1 of 16

Love Is More Than a Feeling

Most people believe love matters. The harder question is what love looks like when relationships become difficult.

How do you love someone who disappoints you?

What do you do when a family member has hurt you?

Does forgiveness mean allowing someone to continue causing harm?

How should the way you treat people change when you follow Jesus?

The final six commandments give practical answers. They protect parents and children, human life, marriage, property, truth, and the human heart.

They also teach one central truth: every person has dignity because every person was created by God.

The Commandments Protect Relationships

Read Exodus 20:12–17 ↗.

The first four commandments teach us how to love the Creator. The final six teach us how to love other people:

  1. Honor your father and mother.
  2. Do not murder.
  3. Do not commit adultery.
  4. Do not steal.
  5. Do not give false testimony.
  6. Do not covet what belongs to another person.

These are more than restrictions. Each commandment protects something valuable.

The fifth protects family relationships.

The sixth protects life.

The seventh protects marriage and trust.

The eighth protects property and honest work.

The ninth protects truth and reputation.

The tenth protects the heart from jealousy and greed.

The Creator cares about how we treat one another.

Every Person Carries God-Given Value

Read Genesis 1:26–27 ↗.

Every human being was made in the Creator’s image.

A person’s value does not come from money, education, health, appearance, influence, race, family background, or ability. Human dignity comes from God.

Read James 2:1–9 ↗.

The Bible condemns favoritism. We cannot claim to love the Creator while treating certain people as less valuable.

Read 1 John 4:20–21 ↗.

Love for God and love for people cannot be separated.

This does not mean approving every choice another person makes. It means telling the truth while still recognizing that person’s God-given worth.

The Fifth Commandment: Honor Your Father and Mother

Read Exodus 20:12 ↗.

The fifth commandment calls us to honor our parents.

Honor includes gratitude, respect, care, and recognition of the sacrifices others have made for us. As parents and grandparents grow older, honor may include helping with practical needs, listening, spending time together, and making sure they are treated with dignity.

Read Proverbs 23:22 ↗ and 1 Timothy 5:4 ↗.

The Creator values relationships between generations. Wisdom, family history, testimony, and practical knowledge can be lost when younger and older people stop listening to one another.

You do not have to agree with your parents about everything to treat them respectfully.

What If a Parent Has Caused Harm?

Some people hear “honor your parents” and feel pain rather than warmth.

A parent may have been absent, addicted, controlling, violent, or abusive. The fifth commandment does not give parents permission to cause harm.

Read Colossians 3:20–21 ↗.

The Bible gives responsibilities to both children and parents. Parents must not use their authority to crush or discourage their children.

Honor does not always mean:

  • Obeying an unsafe demand
  • Hiding abuse
  • Pretending that harm did not happen
  • Allowing someone unlimited access to your life
  • Remaining in a dangerous situation
  • Refusing help from trustworthy people

You can acknowledge the truth, establish healthy boundaries, and still refuse hatred.

In some situations, the most respectful choice is to speak honestly, create distance, or seek help. Forgiveness can begin in your heart even when trust has not yet been restored.

Trust is rebuilt through truth, responsibility, and changed behavior.

The Sixth Commandment: Protect Human Life

Read Exodus 20:13 ↗.

The sixth commandment says, “You shall not murder.”

Human life belongs to the Creator. No individual has the right to treat another person’s life as worthless.

Jesus showed that this commandment reaches beyond physical violence.

Read Matthew 5:21–24 ↗.

Hatred, contempt, and uncontrolled anger can grow from the same root that produces violence.

Anger itself is not always sinful. The Creator becomes angry at injustice, cruelty, and oppression. Anger can alert us that something is wrong.

The danger comes when anger controls us.

Uncontrolled anger may lead to:

  • Threats
  • Cruel words
  • Revenge
  • Physical violence
  • Damaging property
  • Public humiliation
  • Long-term hatred
  • Treating another person as less than human

Read Ephesians 4:26–27 ↗.

Deal with anger before it becomes a place where evil can grow.

How Can You Respond to Anger?

When anger rises:

  1. Pause before speaking or posting.
  2. Move away if the situation could become violent.
  3. Ask the Creator to control your thoughts and actions.
  4. Identify what is beneath the anger.
  5. Speak directly and truthfully when it is safe.
  6. Seek wise help if the conflict is serious.
  7. Pursue justice without seeking personal revenge.

Read Romans 12:17–21 ↗.

Refusing revenge does not mean ignoring wrongdoing. Justice seeks to stop harm and make things right. Revenge seeks to make another person suffer because you suffered.

The Creator calls us to pursue what is right without allowing hatred to reshape our character.

Words Can Also Wound

Read Proverbs 18:21 ↗.

Words can bring life or cause deep harm.

A cruel message, humiliating post, private screenshot, rumor, or angry comment can travel far beyond the moment in which it was created.

Before speaking or posting, ask:

  • Is it true?
  • Is it necessary?
  • Am I trying to help or humiliate?
  • Would I say this if the person were standing beside me?
  • Does this protect human dignity?
  • Will I be at peace if this is shared publicly?

Read Ephesians 4:29 ↗.

Use words that build, heal, correct wisely, and give courage.

The Seventh Commandment: Protect Marriage and Trust

Read Exodus 20:14 ↗.

The seventh commandment says, “You shall not commit adultery.”

The Creator designed sexual intimacy as a gift within the covenant of marriage between a man and a woman.

Read Genesis 2:21–24 ↗ and Matthew 19:4–6 ↗.

Marriage joins two lives through faithfulness, trust, responsibility, and love. Adultery breaks that covenant and often harms spouses, children, families, and communities.

Jesus taught that faithfulness begins before a physical act.

Read Matthew 5:27–28 ↗.

What we repeatedly watch, imagine, and desire shapes the heart.

Sexual integrity includes:

  • Respecting another person’s body
  • Refusing manipulation or pressure
  • Keeping commitments
  • Rejecting pornography
  • Setting wise boundaries while dating
  • Avoiding secret emotional relationships
  • Speaking honestly about intentions
  • Treating people as whole human beings

Another person is never an object to use for pleasure, attention, status, or relief from loneliness.

Why Does the Creator Care About Sexual Choices?

The Creator is not ashamed of the human body. He made it.

Read 1 Corinthians 6:18–20 ↗.

Sexual choices affect the body, emotions, trust, and future relationships. What feels private can produce lasting consequences.

God’s instructions protect intimacy from exploitation, dishonesty, abandonment, and betrayal.

If your sexual past includes choices you regret, you are not beyond forgiveness.

Read 1 Corinthians 6:9–11 ↗.

Jesus can forgive, cleanse, and give you a new beginning. Your past does not have to control your identity or future relationships.

If someone violated your boundaries or abused you, that harm was not your fault. Another person’s sin does not make you dirty or less valuable to the Creator.

The Eighth Commandment: Respect What Belongs to Others

Read Exodus 20:15 ↗.

The eighth commandment says, “You shall not steal.”

Stealing includes taking money or property that does not belong to you. The principle reaches further.

It can include:

  • Refusing to repay what was borrowed
  • Keeping something you know was lost
  • Cheating someone in a sale
  • Failing to pay a worker fairly
  • Taking credit for another person’s work
  • Using work hours dishonestly
  • Copying paid content without permission
  • Exploiting someone who has fewer choices
  • Using power to take land or resources unjustly

Read Leviticus 19:11–13 ↗ and James 5:1–5 ↗.

The Bible applies honesty to individuals, businesses, leaders, and institutions. Greater power creates greater responsibility.

The Creator sees theft even when human laws permit it or powerful people hide it.

What Does Honesty Produce?

Read Ephesians 4:28 ↗.

The Creator calls a person away from stealing and toward honest work and generosity.

The opposite of stealing is more than leaving another person’s property alone. It is becoming someone who can be trusted and who willingly helps people in need.

Honesty builds safety.

When people keep their promises, pay what they owe, return what they borrow, and deal fairly, relationships become stronger.

If you have taken something, repentance may include returning it or repaying what was lost.

Read Luke 19:1–10 ↗.

When Zacchaeus met Jesus, he chose to repay the people he had cheated. Grace changed how he handled money.

The Ninth Commandment: Protect Truth and Reputation

Read Exodus 20:16 ↗.

The ninth commandment says not to give false testimony against another person.

In its original setting, false testimony could cause an innocent person to lose freedom, property, reputation, or life.

Lies still cause damage.

False testimony can include:

  • Making an accusation you know is untrue
  • Leaving out facts to create a false impression
  • Repeating a rumor without checking it
  • Editing someone’s words to change their meaning
  • Lying to protect your reputation
  • Sharing private information to embarrass someone
  • Remaining silent when your truthful words could protect an innocent person

Read Proverbs 6:16–19 ↗.

The Creator hates lies because lies destroy trust and divide people.

What About Gossip?

Gossip can contain true information and still be wrong.

Ask why you are sharing it.

Are you seeking help, protecting someone, or solving a problem? Or are you enjoying the power that comes from exposing another person?

Read Proverbs 11:13 ↗ and Proverbs 16:28 ↗.

A trustworthy person knows how to protect private information.

This does not mean keeping abuse or dangerous behavior secret. If someone is being harmed, speak with a safe person who can help. Protecting a person’s reputation should never become a reason to protect an abuser.

Truth and love work together.

How Should You Handle Conflict?

Jesus gave a clear process.

Read Matthew 18:15–17 ↗.

When someone has wronged you, begin by speaking directly with that person when it is safe and appropriate.

Avoid building a group against someone before giving that person an opportunity to respond.

If the problem cannot be resolved, involve one or two wise and trustworthy people. Serious harm may also require help from appropriate authorities.

The goal is truth, safety, accountability, and restoration.

Online arguments rarely provide all four.

Before making a private conflict public, ask whether you have followed a fair process and whether public disclosure is necessary to protect someone.

The Tenth Commandment: Guard Your Heart

Read Exodus 20:17 ↗.

The tenth commandment says not to covet.

Coveting means allowing an unhealthy desire for what belongs to someone else to control your heart.

You may covet someone’s:

  • Relationship
  • Appearance
  • Home
  • Career
  • Income
  • Education
  • Influence
  • Family
  • Opportunities
  • Online attention

Coveting is different from setting a healthy goal. A goal says, “I am willing to work faithfully toward something good.”

Coveting says, “I cannot be satisfied unless I have what belongs to that person.”

This commandment reaches thoughts and desires that other people may never see. It shows that the Creator wants to transform the heart.

Comparison Can Steal Your Peace

Social media allows you to see the most polished moments of hundreds of lives.

You may compare someone else’s carefully selected image with your entire unedited life.

That comparison can produce envy, shame, resentment, or the feeling that you are falling behind.

Read 2 Corinthians 10:12 ↗ and Philippians 4:11–13 ↗.

Contentment does not mean giving up on growth. It means your peace is not controlled by what someone else has.

The Creator’s path for another person may look different from His path for you.

Gratitude weakens envy.

Each day, name specific gifts the Creator has already placed in your life. Thank Him for another person’s success without treating it as proof of your failure.

Who Is Your Neighbor?

A religious leader once asked Jesus this question.

Read Luke 10:25–37 ↗.

Jesus answered with the story of a man who was attacked and left beside the road. Respected religious people passed without helping him. A Samaritan, a member of a group viewed with hostility, stopped and cared for him.

The true neighbor was the person who showed mercy.

Your neighbor includes more than people who look like you, agree with you, belong to your family, or share your history.

Love does not require ignoring truth or injustice. It refuses to let difference become an excuse for cruelty.

Read Micah 6:8 ↗.

The Creator calls us to act justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with Him.

Does Forgiveness Remove Accountability?

Read Colossians 3:12–13 ↗.

The Creator calls us to forgive because He has forgiven us.

Forgiveness releases personal revenge and places final judgment in God’s hands.

Forgiveness does not always mean:

  • Immediate trust
  • Removing wise boundaries
  • Returning to an unsafe relationship
  • Pretending the harm was small
  • Blocking legal consequences
  • Refusing professional help
  • Allowing the behavior to continue

Reconciliation requires truth and participation from both sides. Forgiveness can begin in one heart even when reconciliation is not yet possible.

Jesus combines mercy with justice. We should do the same.

Love Must Become Action

Read 1 John 3:16–18 ↗.

Love is more than kind words or warm feelings. It becomes visible through action.

Love may look like:

  • Listening carefully
  • Keeping a promise
  • Showing up when someone is grieving
  • Sharing food or resources
  • Defending someone being mistreated
  • Apologizing without excuses
  • Helping an older relative
  • Encouraging someone who feels forgotten
  • Speaking truth with kindness
  • Making your home and relationships safer
  • Giving time without expecting attention

You do not need a large platform to make a real difference.

The Creator can use ordinary acts of faithfulness to bring healing to a family or community.

Your Choices Affect More Than You

Modern life often treats every choice as private: “This is my life, and it affects only me.”

The Bible shows that our lives are connected.

A lie can divide a family. An addiction can affect children and partners. Faithfulness can create safety. One honest apology can begin repairing years of distance.

Read 1 Corinthians 12:25–27 ↗.

The Creator calls us to care about how our choices affect other people.

Following Jesus includes personal decisions, but it never ends with the individual. The Creator changes us so that our lives can become a blessing to others.

Think About It

Write your answers in your own words.

  1. Which of the final six commandments feels most relevant to your life right now?
  2. What does honoring a parent look like when the relationship is healthy?
  3. How can someone establish boundaries while refusing hatred?
  4. What usually happens when anger controls your words or actions?
  5. What boundaries could protect trust in your present or future relationship?
  6. Is there anything you need to return, repay, or make right?
  7. Have you repeated information about someone without knowing whether it was true?
  8. What comparison most often steals your peace?
  9. Who might the Creator be asking you to treat as a neighbor?
  10. What practical act of love can you offer this week?

Try This During the Coming Week

Focus on one commandment each day:

  • Day 1: Exodus 20:12 ↗ and Ephesians 6:1–4 ↗
  • Day 2: Exodus 20:13 ↗ and Matthew 5:21–24 ↗
  • Day 3: Exodus 20:14 ↗ and Matthew 5:27–30 ↗
  • Day 4: Exodus 20:15 ↗ and Ephesians 4:28 ↗
  • Day 5: Exodus 20:16 ↗ and Ephesians 4:25–32 ↗
  • Day 6: Exodus 20:17 ↗ and Philippians 4:10–13 ↗
  • Day 7: Luke 10:25–37 ↗

After each reading, write down:

  • What relationship or human need does this command protect?
  • Is there an attitude or action I need to change?
  • Is there harm I need to repair?
  • What act of love can I practice today?

Choose one person each day and pray for that person by name. Ask the Creator to show you one practical way to treat that person with dignity.

A Prayer You Can Pray

Creator God, thank You for giving every person dignity and value. Teach me to love people through my choices as well as my words. Help me honor my family with wisdom, control my anger, protect life, remain faithful, act honestly, speak truth, and become content with what You provide. Show me where I have caused harm and give me courage to make things right. Help me forgive without ignoring truth or safety. Fill me with the love of Jesus so that my life brings healing to my family, relationships, and community. Amen.

Remember This

The final six commandments protect human relationships.

Every person has dignity because every person was made by the Creator.

Honoring parents does not require hiding abuse or remaining unsafe.

The command against murder also confronts hatred and destructive anger.

Sexual intimacy belongs within the marriage covenant between a man and a woman.

The Creator calls us to respect property, labor, and what belongs to others.

Truth protects reputations, relationships, and justice.

Forgiveness releases revenge but does not remove wise boundaries or accountability.

Contentment protects the heart from envy and comparison.

Love for the Creator becomes visible in the way we treat people.
